Ben Jonson. A playwright, poet, and critic who was Shakespeare's contemporary and rival, yet became his greatest champion and friend.

Born in fifteen seventy-two, Jonson came to London as a young man and worked his way up through humble roles. He was a bricklayer, an actor, and then a playwright, rising to prominence in the early sixteen hundreds. His path was unconventional, but his talent was undeniable.

What made Jonson stand out was his satirical genius. He wrote comedies built on complex schemes and morally corrupt characters, people driven by obsession and vice. These weren't simple stories. They were intricate explorations of human folly that revealed how greed, lust, and vanity could consume a person entirely.

Volpone, which premiered in sixteen oh five, is considered his masterpiece. The title character is a wealthy Venetian merchant who feigns terminal illness to trick his greedy acquaintances into lavishing gifts upon him. It's a brilliant satire, a play about how easily people's base desires can be manipulated when they believe there's profit to be made.

The Alchemist, which came five years later in sixteen ten, stands as his equal in acclaim. Set in plague-ridden London, it follows a con artist and his cohorts who pose as an alchemist and his assistant. They dupe gullible victims into paying for promises of gold and spiritual transformation. It's the perfect complement to Volpone—another masterwork about schemes and deception.

Jonson pioneered what became known as the comedy of humours. In these plays, characters embody excessive traits, pathological obsessions really—avarice, vanity, lust, pedantry taken to extremes. This approach to comedy influenced English drama for centuries to come.

Unlike Shakespeare, Jonson was deeply learned in classical literature and theory. He knew Latin and classical authors thoroughly. He consciously imitated Roman comedies by Plautus and Terence, building his own works on classical models. This elevated English comedy to classical dignity, proving that English dramatists could draw on the full weight of ancient tradition.

Beyond the theatre, Jonson was a celebrated poet in his own right. He also wrote masques—elaborate theatrical entertainments combining music, dance, and spectacle for the royal court. These works showcased both his learning and his wit.

During their lifetimes, Jonson was fiercely competitive with Shakespeare. But when Shakespeare died in sixteen sixteen, Jonson became his greatest posthumous advocate. He edited the First Folio in sixteen twenty-three, the collection that preserved so many of Shakespeare's plays. Without it, many of those works would have been lost. Jonson wrote a prefatory poem praising Shakespeare as "not of an age, but for all time"—a tribute that has endured for four centuries.

Jonson emerged during the height of English Renaissance drama, when theatrical competition was intense. While Shakespeare was beloved for his emotional depth and linguistic beauty, Jonson was admired for his intellectual rigor, his classical learning, and his satirical bite. He represented a different ideal of dramatic art, one grounded in classical precedent and rational comic structure rather than romantic imagination. Yet the two men respected each other.

His own reputation dimmed somewhat in later centuries, overshadowed by the Romantic era's intense admiration for Shakespeare. But his plays have experienced sustained rediscovery and revaluation. His impact on English comedy—its satirical tradition, its use of character-based humour, its intellectual ambitions—remains profound.
